body:
What are microwaves?

Microwaves are a form of electromagnetic radiation. They belong to the same broad electromagnetic spectrum as radio waves, visible light and X-rays, but they have different wavelengths and frequencies.

Microwaves are non-ionizing radiation. This means that an individual microwave photon does not have enough energy to remove a tightly bound electron from an atom in the way that ionizing radiation, such as X-rays, can.

Non-ionizing does not mean that microwaves carry no energy. Microwaves can transfer energy to materials that absorb them. A microwave oven uses this property to heat food.

How a microwave oven works

A microwave oven contains a device called a magnetron, which produces microwaves. The microwaves travel into the cooking chamber and reflect from its metal interior.

Food absorbs part of this electromagnetic energy. Water molecules in food are particularly important because they are polar molecules: the distribution of electrical charge within each molecule is uneven.

The rapidly changing electric field of the microwaves makes these molecules attempt to change their orientation repeatedly. Their motion and interactions with surrounding molecules convert the absorbed electromagnetic energy into heat.

This process is commonly described as dielectric heating. In simple terms, electrical energy is used to generate electromagnetic waves, and the food absorbs some of their energy as heat.

Does a microwave cook food from the inside out?

No. Microwave energy can penetrate some distance into food, so heating is not limited to the outermost surface. However, penetration is not unlimited.

In a thick piece of food, microwaves heat the outer regions and some material below the surface. Heat then moves further towards the centre by conduction, which is the transfer of thermal energy through matter from hotter regions to cooler regions.

Therefore, the popular statement that microwave ovens always cook food from the inside out is incorrect.

Why different materials behave differently

  • Food containing water: Absorbs microwave energy and becomes hot.
  • Metal surfaces: Reflect microwaves. This is why the cooking chamber has a metal interior.
  • Suitable glass and ceramic containers: Generally allow much of the microwave energy to reach the food, although they may become hot through contact with the heated food.
  • Plastic containers: Should be used only when suitable for microwave cooking; some plastics can soften, melt or be unsuitable for food heating.

Ordinary metal utensils and aluminium foil should generally not be placed inside a microwave oven unless the manufacturer specifically permits their use. Metal objects can interfere with heating and may cause sparking or other problems.

Safety and common misconceptions

Microwave-heated food does not become radioactive. Microwave energy is converted into heat as the food absorbs it. Once the oven stops generating microwaves, there is no process that turns ordinary food into a radioactive substance.

Microwave heating can be uneven. Some regions may be hotter than others, especially in thick foods. Stirring, turning and allowing food to stand after heating can help redistribute heat.

A microwave oven should not be used if its door, hinges, latches or seals are damaged. The door and enclosure are designed to prevent unsafe leakage of microwave energy during operation.

Radiation and radioactivity are different concepts. Microwaves are electromagnetic radiation. Their use in cooking does not make food radioactive. However, excessive exposure to microwave energy can heat body tissue and cause injury.

Prelims focus

  • Microwaves are electromagnetic waves and are non-ionizing.
  • A magnetron generates microwaves in a conventional microwave oven.
  • Food heats by absorbing microwave energy, particularly through interactions involving polar water molecules.
  • Metal reflects microwaves; suitable microwave-safe containers allow energy to reach the food.
  • Microwave-heated food does not become radioactive.
  • Trap: Thick food is not necessarily cooked from the inside out; heat also reaches its centre by conduction.

[U.S. Food and Drug Administration, Microwave Ovens, sections What is Microwave Radiation?, Cooking with Microwaves, Microwave Ovens and Health, and Tips on Safe Microwave Oven Operation, consulted 3 November 2026; NCERT, Class 7, Science, Chapter 4, Heat, 2018–19 edition, for the foundational distinction between temperature and heat transfer.]

body:
The basic principle

An induction cooktop is an electrical cooking appliance that heats suitable cookware through electromagnetic induction.

Electromagnetic induction occurs when a changing magnetic field produces an electromotive force (induced voltage) in a nearby conductor. In an induction cooktop, this principle is used to produce heating within the base of a cooking vessel.

Unlike a gas stove, an induction cooktop does not require a flame. Unlike a conventional resistance-based electric hotplate, its main method of heating is not to make an exposed heating element hot and then transfer that heat to the vessel.

How induction cooking works

  1. An alternating electric current passes through a coil located beneath the cooktop surface.
  2. The alternating current produces a changing magnetic field around the coil.
  3. When a suitable cooking vessel is placed above the coil, the changing magnetic field induces electrical currents in the vessel's base.
  4. The induced currents produce heat in the vessel because its material resists their flow.
  5. Heat passes from the hot vessel to the food or water inside it.

In induction cooking, the cooking vessel is heated directly by the induction process. The food is then heated through contact with the hot vessel and its contents.

Why cookware compatibility matters

An induction cooktop generally requires cookware with a suitable ferromagnetic base. Ferromagnetic materials, such as iron, interact strongly with magnetic fields and are suitable for this type of cooking.

Common examples of suitable cookware include cast-iron pans and many steel or stainless-steel vessels. However, not every stainless-steel vessel is induction-compatible, because stainless steel has different compositions and magnetic properties.

Plain aluminium, copper or glass vessels without a suitable induction-compatible base generally will not work on an ordinary induction cooktop. Some vessels made mainly from these materials can work if they have a specially designed compatible base.

A simple practical test is to place a household magnet against the bottom of the vessel. If the magnet sticks firmly, the vessel is likely to be suitable for induction cooking.

Microwave oven and induction cooktop: The essential distinction

FeatureMicrowave ovenInduction cooktop
Main principleAbsorption of microwave electromagnetic energyElectromagnetic induction
What is heated directly?Food absorbs microwave energyCompatible cooking vessel
Role of cookwareSuitable container allows microwaves to reach foodMagnetic compatibility of the vessel's base is important
How food receives heatMicrowave absorption and subsequent heat transferHeat transfer from the hot vessel

Both appliances use electricity and electromagnetic principles, but their heating mechanisms differ. A microwave oven generates electromagnetic waves that are absorbed by food. An induction cooktop creates a changing magnetic field that produces electrical currents and heat in suitable cookware.

Advantages and a safety qualification

Induction cooking can be efficient because energy is transferred directly to the cookware instead of first heating a large burner. Heating can respond quickly when power is changed.

However, the statement that an induction cooktop never becomes hot is incorrect. Although its principal heating process occurs in the vessel, the cooktop surface can become hot through contact with the heated vessel.

Prelims focus

  • Induction cooking depends on electromagnetic induction.
  • An alternating current in a coil produces a changing magnetic field.
  • Induced currents heat the compatible cooking vessel.
  • Cast iron and many magnetic steel vessels are induction-compatible.
  • A magnet sticking to the vessel's base is a useful compatibility test.
  • Trap: A microwave oven mainly heats food through absorption of microwaves; an induction cooktop heats compatible cookware through induced currents.

[NCERT, Class 7, Science, Chapter 14, Electric Current and its Effects, printed pp. 164–169, 2018–19 edition, for the heating and magnetic effects of electric current; U.S. Department of Energy, Making the Switch to Induction Stoves or Cooktops, section How it Works, 11 May 2023, consulted 3 November 2026; ENERGY STAR, Electric Cooking Products, section Buying Guidance, consulted 3 November 2026.]

title: Induction Cooktops: Heating a Pan Through Electromagnetic Induction

body:
What is tyre pressure?

A vehicle tyre contains air under pressure. Tyre pressure is the pressure exerted by the compressed air inside the tyre against its inner surfaces.

Air is a gas, and gases exert pressure in all directions. When air is pumped into a tyre, it pushes against the tyre's inner walls. The pressurised air, together with the tyre's structure, helps the tyre retain its shape and support the vehicle.

In physics, pressure means the force acting normally on a surface per unit area.

\(P=\frac{F}{A}\)

Here, \(P\) represents pressure, \(F\) represents the force perpendicular to the surface, and \(A\) represents the area over which the force acts. The SI unit of pressure is the pascal (Pa). Vehicle tyre pressure is commonly stated in kilopascals (kPa) or pounds per square inch (psi).

Why tyre inflation affects vehicle movement

A tyre touches the road over a region called its contact patch. The size and shape of this region depend on factors including tyre inflation, the load on the wheel and the tyre's construction.

When a vehicle starts moving, turns or brakes, it depends on friction between its tyres and the road. Friction provides the grip needed for acceleration, steering and stopping.

Tyre pressure influences how the tyre deforms and how its tread meets the road. Therefore, correct inflation is important for steering, braking, comfort, tyre life and energy consumption.

Underinflation, correct inflation and overinflation

Underinflation means that the tyre pressure is below the level recommended for the vehicle and its operating conditions. An underinflated tyre generally deforms more while rolling. This repeated bending produces additional heat and can increase rolling resistance. It may also cause irregular tyre wear and adversely affect handling.

Overinflation means that the tyre pressure is above the recommended level. It can make the tyre less able to absorb bumps and can change the distribution of contact between the tread and road. Excessive pressure may contribute to uneven wear and unsuitable handling characteristics.

Correct inflation means maintaining the pressure recommended by the vehicle manufacturer for the relevant tyre size and load condition. It is not simply the highest pressure the tyre can withstand.

More pressure does not automatically mean better road grip. Grip also depends on tyre condition, tread, road surface, load and temperature. The correct aim is the manufacturer's recommended inflation pressure, not the highest possible value.

How temperature changes tyre pressure

When a vehicle is driven, its tyres warm up because of repeated deformation and interaction with the road. As the air inside becomes warmer, its pressure generally rises.

Similarly, a reduction in air temperature generally causes tyre pressure to fall. This explains why pressure readings may differ between a cool morning and a hot afternoon.

The recommended inflation value is ordinarily a cold tyre pressure. It should not be interpreted as the target reading immediately after a long drive when the tyres are hot.

Checking tyre pressure correctly

  1. Find the pressure recommended by the vehicle manufacturer, usually on the vehicle's tyre-information label or in its owner's manual.
  2. Measure pressure with a suitable tyre-pressure gauge when the tyres are cold. A commonly used condition is that the vehicle has not been driven for at least 3 hours.
  3. Compare the reading with the recommended cold pressure for that tyre position and load condition.
  4. Adjust the pressure appropriately and recheck it. The front and rear tyres may have different recommended values.

The maximum inflation pressure marked on the tyre's sidewall is not necessarily the vehicle manufacturer's recommended operating pressure. A tyre-pressure monitoring system may warn the driver about significantly low pressure, but it does not replace regular checks with a gauge.

Tyre tread and wet-road friction

Tyre tread is the patterned outer surface that touches the road. Its grooves help maintain traction, particularly by allowing water to move away from the contact region on wet roads.

Good tread condition and correct tyre pressure are related but different requirements. A properly inflated tyre with severely worn tread may still have poor wet-road grip. Likewise, a tyre with adequate tread can perform poorly when incorrectly inflated.

Connecting the everyday technologies

The devices in this lesson use different scientific principles for different purposes. An LED converts electrical energy into light through electroluminescence. FASTag uses radio waves for identification and electronic payment. A lithium-ion cell stores and releases chemical energy. A microwave oven transfers electromagnetic energy directly to food. An induction cooktop produces heat in compatible cookware through electromagnetic induction. Tyre inflation applies the principles of gas pressure, while road grip depends on friction.

Prelims focus

  • Tyre pressure results from compressed air exerting pressure on the tyre's inner surfaces.
  • Pressure is force per unit area; its SI unit is the pascal.
  • Vehicle tyre pressure is commonly measured in kPa or psi.
  • Underinflation can increase tyre deformation, heat production and rolling resistance.
  • Tyre pressure should be checked cold against the vehicle manufacturer's recommendation.
  • Trap: The maximum pressure printed on a tyre's sidewall is not necessarily the correct inflation pressure for the vehicle.

[NCERT, Class 8, Science, Chapter 11, Force and Pressure, printed pp. 137–140, 2018–19 edition; NCERT, Class 8, Science, Chapter 12, Friction, printed pp. 146–152, 2018–19 edition; U.S. National Highway Traffic Safety Administration, Tires, sections Maintenance, Tire Pressure, Tire Tread and Tire Pressure Monitoring System, consulted 3 November 2026; U.S. National Highway Traffic Safety Administration, Tires, section Maintaining Proper Tire Pressure, consulted 3 November 2026.]
